paras: The attempted lynching of Robert Williams took place at the city jail in Lynchburg, Virginia, at about 1 a.m. on August 15, 1920, when a crowd of 200 to 300 or more tried to seize Williams, a Black man accused of assaulting Annie Ross, a Swedish-born masseuse. Police had already moved Williams out of the jail, and officers dispersed the crowd and arrested two men, who were fined and jailed for unlawful assembly and riot. In September a jury convicted Williams after eight minutes and he was sentenced to death.

According to a Lynchburg dispatch of August 7, Ross, a governess, was seized in the Rivermont section at about 11:30 the night before, dragged about 200 yards and assaulted; she said her attacker struck her with a wrench. Bloodhounds followed a trail to Chambersville, "a negro suburb," where Williams, called "Alabama Red," was arrested while denying guilt; officers said they found a muddy wrench in his home.

Just after a caller asked police headquarters whether the relief men had left the station, the Richmond Times-Dispatch reported, the crowd "swooped down on the jail." Williams was not there, because Chief of Police John Seay had taken him from his cell shortly before and kept him hidden until the last night train to Roanoke. City Sergeant Tyree, the jailer, and a few policemen met the crowd at the jail gate. In the Washington Herald's account, a masked leader shouted "We want Williams," and an officer pulled the handkerchief away, "revealing a prominent citizen of Lynchburg," and pushed him into the cell Williams had just left.

The Times-Dispatch likewise said Tyree unmasked and jailed "one of the leaders," but described the crowd as "leaderless" and made up mostly of young men. Officers summoned by police telegraph arrived, and after O. H. Morris and Aubrey Foster were locked up the crowd dispersed, not knowing that Williams was gone. Police and Mayor Royston Jester Jr. said Williams confessed to them that morning before he was taken to the Roanoke jail.

A Bible class taught by Judge Frank P. Christian and the Rotary Club telegraphed the vacationing judge to urge a special term to try Williams, but Christian ruled that he had no power to call one before the September term. On August 18 Morris and Foster were convicted in Police Court of "unlawful assembly, and riot," fined $25 each and sentenced to ten days in jail. No report of further arrests appears in the coverage.

A week later a Washington Herald report said it was "universally admitted" that returning Williams for trial without military protection would be unwise. Williams was indicted on September 7 and brought from Roanoke for a trial kept unannounced for fear of another attempt to take him. He pleaded not guilty and repudiated the signed confessions held by police, the defense neither cross-examined nor argued, and he was sentenced to be electrocuted on November 13.

The Times-Dispatch covered the episode most fully, opening with a front-page report headlined "Mob Attempts to Lynch a Negro at Lynchburg." Its next report called the crowd "would-be lynchers" but led with the police account under "Negro Confesses He Attacked White Woman." The Washington Herald featured the unmasking ("Jailer Hides Man From Mob"), while the Washington Times reprinted the Times-Dispatch text and headlined the verdict "Jury Sentences Negro to Death in 8 Minutes."

Among Black newspapers, the episode appeared only in the Richmond Planet of August 21, which reprinted the first Times-Dispatch dispatch almost word for word under "Mob Attempts to Lynch Man at Lynchburg." The Planet capitalized "Negro" and added no comment, and no Black-press report of the confession or the trial was found.

The crowd was put at "200 to 300" in the fuller Times-Dispatch account, at 300 in its first report, and at "over 300" in the Washington Herald. The assault was dated to the night of August 6 in the next day's dispatch, the account closest in time, but to August 8 in the report of the verdict. The confession rests on statements by the police and the mayor, while Williams denied guilt at his arrest and repudiated the confessions at trial.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Williams
bases: A crowd of 200 to 300 or more went to the Lynchburg jail to take Robert Williams, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, 'for a lynching', and was dispersed by police after he had been removed (A2, A3, A6).
The crowd of 200 to 300 or more acted without authority on a criminal-assault accusation, but Williams had been moved to Roanoke and no one was killed; it was an attempted lynching (A2, A3, A15).

The Times-Dispatch dispatches (A2, A3) and the separately worded Washington Herald report (A6) agree on the crowd at the jail, the removal of Williams and the arrests, and the Police Court convictions (A10) confirm them.

accounts.label: Times-Dispatch Lynchburg correspondent
accounts.gist: A leaderless crowd of 200 to 300, mostly young men, went to the jail at about 1 a.m.; Tyree unmasked and jailed a leader, Morris and Foster were arrested, and the crowd left without knowing Williams had been moved.

accounts.label: Washington Herald dispatch
accounts.gist: A crowd of over 300 attacked the jail; its masked leader demanded Williams, was unmasked as 'a prominent citizen of Lynchburg' and locked in Williams's empty cell; one more arrest followed.

accounts.label: Police and mayor
accounts.gist: Williams confessed to police and to Mayor Jester early on August 15 before being taken to Roanoke.

accounts.label: Williams at trial
accounts.gist: Williams pleaded not guilty and repudiated the signed confessions held by police.

accounts.label: Black press reprint
accounts.gist: The Richmond Planet repeated the first Times-Dispatch dispatch: a mob of 300 tried to take Williams from the jail and was routed by police.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Mob Attempts to Lynch a Negro' and called the crowd 'would-be lynchers', but its follow-up led with 'Negro Confesses He Attacked White Woman' and treated the police account of guilt as settled.
The Washington Herald told the story as a jailer outwitting the mob ('Jailer Hides Man From Mob'), naming the leader only as 'a prominent citizen'.
The Washington Times ran the Times-Dispatch text under 'Foil Jail Mob, Arrest Chiefs' and later headlined the verdict 'Jury Sentences Negro to Death in 8 Minutes'.
The Richmond Planet reprinted the first dispatch under 'Mob Attempts to Lynch Man at Lynchburg', with 'Negro' capitalized and no comment.

record_check.dossier: Crowd estimated at 200 to 300 or more; it was met at the jail gate and dispersed; no report says it broke in (the headline says it 'tried to break into jail').
Crowd mostly of young men; O. H. Morris and Aubrey Foster arrested and convicted of unlawful assembly and riot
Crowd at the jail demanding Williams; brief confrontation at the gate, no damage reported
Williams indicted Sept. 7, convicted by a jury after eight minutes and sentenced to electrocution on Nov. 13; mob members fined $25 and jailed ten days

Robert Williams, alias 'Alabama Red', described as 'a negro' / 'colored'; not harmed, having been removed from the jail before the crowd arrived
Accused of criminally assaulting Miss Annie Ross, a Swedish-born masseuse and governess in the home of E. F. Haley, in Rivermont on the night of August 6
A crowd 'composed mostly of young men'; O. H. Morris and Aubrey Foster arrested; the Washington Herald said the masked leader was 'a prominent citizen of Lynchburg'
Williams pleaded not guilty and repudiated his signed confessions; jury found him guilty after eight minutes; sentenced to be electrocuted at the state penitentiary in Richmond on November 13
